entries:
From Middle High German brille, berille, from berillus (“beryl”), from Latin beryllus (“beryl”). Compare dialectal English brills (“spectacles”).
The "toilet seat" sense is derived in analogy with the usually round shape of spectacle frames surrounding the glass, just as a toilet seat surrounds the toilet hole.
senses: glasses, spectacles (frames bearing two lenses worn in front of the eyes to correct vision)
goggles (protective eyewear set in a flexible frame to fit snugly against the face)
Ellipsis of Klobrille (“toilet seat”) (hinged, contoured seat with a hole in the middle, of a toilet)
nasal cannula for oxygen (clear plastic tubes for the delivery of oxygen to the nose)
strong/mixed nominative/accusative neuter singular of interventionistisch
strong/mixed nominative masculine singular comparative degree
strong genitive/dative feminine singular comparative degree

entries: wie sie sehen, sehen sie nichts
Literally, “as you can see, you can’t see anything”. First said by German TV host Hans-Joachim Kulenkampff when the lights went out during a live show.
senses: wie sie sehen, sehen sie nichts
Said when something to be shown or presented cannot be seen properly, e.g. due to a technical problem, fog, etc.
